title: Understanding the Terminology

sections.normalized_html: Remember that a system is consistent if it has a solution. So, the idea that a system of equations with no solution is inconsistent probably makes sense to you.

sections.readable_text: To help understand consistent dependent vs. consistent independent, we'll look at some concrete examples:

sections.normalized_html:
• First, consider the following system. [MATH: {3x − y = − 2; 6x − 2y = − 4] This system has infinitely many solutions corresponding to the fact that the two lines coincide.

    In a previous lesson, we saw that the set of all solutions [MATH: ({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}})] can be expressed as [MATH: ({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{3x+2}})] where [MATH: {\color{blue}{x}}] is any number. Consequently, any [MATH: {\color{red}{y}}]-value in our solution is dependent on a corresponding [MATH: {\color{blue}{x}}]-value. Thus, the system of equations is consistent-dependent.

  • Next, we consider the following system: [MATH: {y = 2x + 1; y = 1 − x] This system has a single solution corresponding to the unique intersection point of the two lines.

    The unique solution [MATH: ({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}})] is given by the single point [MATH: ({\color{blue}{0}},{\color{red}{1}}).] In this case, the components of the solution do not depend on [MATH: x] or [MATH: y.] Thus, the system of equations is consistent-independent.
